explanations.explanation: Paul, the apostle who wrote this letter, asks, "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" He puts it right between "Am I not an apostle?" and "Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord?" Four questions, and he doesn't stumble on a single one. I can barely get through a recipe without losing my place.

Abraham, the man God called to leave his homeland (Genesis 12:1), is a great name, but Paul doesn't ask about him here. His question is, "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" It's a big name that landed in the wrong spot on the counter, friend. Paul keeps his eyes on the Lord.

Elijah, a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 18:36), has a big story, but he isn't who Paul brings up. Paul asks, "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" Nice try, though. That was a solid guess, like grabbing the right cookie cutter for the wrong batch.

explanations.answer: They themselves are the seal of it
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord." He doesn't point to a paper or a person, he points right at the Corinthians. It's like a sealed cookie box. The seal is on the box itself, and the Corinthians are Paul's seal.

explanations.answer: The other apostles vouched for him
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that here. What he says is, "For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord." The proof he points to is standing right in front of him, the Corinthians themselves. I think a man who can point at the people in the room doesn't need a reference.

explanations.answer: He showed them a letter from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No letter comes out in this passage. Paul says, "You are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord." The Corinthians are the proof, no paperwork needed. Picture a man reaching into his pocket for a letter and instead just turning around and pointing at the crowd.

Paul asks, "Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord's brothers and Cephas?" Cephas is Peter (John 1:42). So Paul is pointing at the other apostles and asking what's fair for himself and Barnabas. Notice he calls her a believing wife, so the text says she shares the faith.

Paul's question isn't about a servant. He asks about taking along "a believing wife." It's a fair guess when you picture an apostle on the road, but the text names a wife. I'd love a helper like that in my bakery, though.

No guard shows up in Paul's question. He asks about taking along "a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord's brothers and Cephas." A guard would be a lot of mustache-twirling drama for a simple question. Paul keeps it plain and asks about a wife.

Paul asks, "Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?" Barnabas is Paul's partner on the road. He asks it as a question, and he's pointing at the other apostles. He's asking if the two of them got stuck with the day jobs.

The text really does say it. Paul asks, "Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?" Barnabas is Paul's partner on the road. So Paul puts both of them in that question, and he's asking if they're the only ones.

explanations.answer: A worker shares in what he works for
explanations.explanation: That's it. The soldier gets paid for his service, the vineyard planter eats the fruit and the shepherd drinks the milk. Paul lines up three jobs, and each worker gets something from the work. Three questions and one answer, and the answer is in every one.

explanations.answer: A worker should never complain at all
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about complaining in these three questions. Each one asks about a worker getting something from his work: a soldier's pay, a vineyard's fruit, a flock's milk. I'll admit I've complained about a dough shortage once or twice. Paul isn't talking about that.

explanations.answer: Hard work is always its own reward
explanations.explanation: It sounds nice, but that's not what Paul asks. His workers all get something back: the vineyard planter eats of its fruit, and the shepherd drinks of the flock's milk. If hard work were its own reward, nobody would need the fruit. Paul's point is that the worker shares in what he works for.

Paul says, "For it is written in the Law of Moses: 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.'" Moses was Israel's leader. So Paul isn't just giving his own opinion. He goes straight to the Law to back up what he's saying.

The text says this one. Paul writes, "For it is written in the Law of Moses: 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.'" Moses was Israel's leader. Paul uses this line to show that the Law agrees with what he's been saying.

Paul says, "when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest." He says this was written for us. So the plowman and the thresher don't just work, they expect a share of what comes in.

Praise sounds nice, but Paul's text says harvest. The plowman and the thresher "should also expect to share in the harvest." It's a bit like a farmer working all season and getting a nice round of applause instead of a share. Paul has the harvest in mind.

Rest sounds lovely after all that plowing, and I've earned some myself. But Paul says the plowman and the thresher "should also expect to share in the harvest." The text puts the harvest in that spot. They're expecting a share of what the work brings in.

Paul asks, "If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?" Spiritual seed on one side, a material harvest on the other. He ties it right back to the farm talk about the plowman and the thresher.

Heavenly is a good word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says, "is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?" The seed he sowed is spiritual, and the harvest he asks about is material. I think that contrast is the whole point of the question.

A hidden harvest sounds mysterious, like cookies tucked behind the flour sack. Paul's word is "material." He asks, "is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?" It's a plain, everyday kind of harvest.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "But we did not exercise this right." He argues that he has it all the more, then says he didn't use it. It's like a man with a whole bakery of cookies waiting and he says he hasn't touched a crumb.

Paul says, "But we did not exercise this right." He just made a big case that he has it, and then he says he didn't use it. That's the twist in the verse. He argues he has the right, and he puts it down.

explanations.answer: So he wouldn't hinder the gospel of Christ
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ." Anything, friend. That's not a small word, and he picked it on purpose. He has the right and he puts it down, because the gospel matters more to him.

explanations.answer: So no one in Corinth would call him greedy
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason. The text says, "we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ." That's the reason he gives, and I won't put another one in his mouth. I think he'd say what he meant.

explanations.answer: So the Corinthians would owe him even more
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says. Paul says, "we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ." Nothing in it is about building up a debt. The reason he gives is the gospel.

Paul says, "the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel." He starts with temple workers eating of the temple's food, then says the Lord set up the same kind of thing for gospel preachers. It's a pattern, friend. The workers get their living from the work they do.

Guarding the city is a real job, but it's not in Paul's line. He says, "the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel." The group he names is gospel preachers. City guards didn't get a seat at this table.

Paul's line is about those who work in the temple, not those who build it. The group he names next is "those who preach the gospel." Builders and servers are different crews, like the guy who bought the oven and the one who bakes. Paul says the Lord prescribed this for gospel preachers.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me." He builds all those arguments and then says he isn't asking for any of it. He argues like a lawyer and asks for nothing.

Paul says it plainly: "And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me." He built the whole case, and he's not collecting on it. It's like me spending all morning on a cookie box and handing it to someone else.

Paul says, "I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach." Then he adds, "Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!" So he doesn't treat preaching as something to brag about. He treats it as something he has to do.
That's the opposite of where Paul's going. He says, "I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach." Paid would be the very right he says he didn't use. His word is obligated.

Trained is a decent guess, and I'll admit I like the sound of it. But Paul says, "I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach." The word is obligated. He's talking about a duty, not his training.

explanations.answer: Offering the gospel free of charge
explanations.explanation: Paul says his reward is "That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it." He has the rights, and he doesn't spend them. The reward he names is giving it away free.

Paul doesn't say that. His reward is "That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge." Honor from every church would be a nice thing, but it isn't the reward he names. His answer is giving the gospel away free.

explanations.answer: Getting a home of his own
explanations.explanation: A home sounds pretty nice, and I've lived in a drawer, so I get it. But Paul says his reward is "That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge." The text doesn't mention a house at all. His reward is the free offer itself.

Paul says, "Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible." It sounds backward, and it is. Free, and then a slave to everyone. He gives the reason too, which is to win as many as possible.

The text says it. Paul writes, "Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible." That's the backward part, friend. He's free, and he makes himself a slave to everyone.

Paul says he's "not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ." He becomes like one without the law for those without it, yet he doesn't leave God's law behind. He says he's under the law of Christ.

The Medes don't show up anywhere in this passage. Paul says he's "not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ." That's the law he names. I'd say the Medes got a whole lot of attention for a law nobody mentioned.

No king gets a mention in Paul's sentence. He says he's "not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ." So the law he names is Christ's. A king's law would be a different kind of cookie altogether.
Paul says, "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some." That's the goal behind all the becoming. Not some of the means, friend, all possible means.
Impress is a fun guess, but it's not Paul's word. He says, "so that by all possible means I might save some." His aim isn't a show. It's saving some.

Correct sounds like something a teacher would say, but Paul's word is "save." He says, "so that by all possible means I might save some." That's what all the becoming is for. I'd say it's a higher goal than fixing people up.

Paul says, "I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings." Everything he just described, becoming all things to all people, is for the gospel. And he says he hopes to share in its blessings himself.

explanations.answer: To be known in every city
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says he does all this "for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings." Being known everywhere isn't in the verse. His hope is to share in the gospel's blessings.

explanations.answer: To rest from all his work
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds lovely, and I'd take a nap on a cookie sheet right now. But Paul says he does it "so that I may share in its blessings." The text doesn't name rest. The blessings of the gospel are what he hopes to share in.
Paul says the opposite. He writes, "Run in such a way as to take the prize." So he sets up a race where only one wins, then tells them to run to win. Nobody gets a seat on the bench.
Paul says, "Run in such a way as to take the prize." Only one receives it, and he still says to run. He doesn't tell them to sit down, he tells them to run like they mean it.
Paul says the athletes "do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable." Imperishable means it doesn't perish. One crown fades, and the other one doesn't.
Gold sounds fancy, but Paul never says that. He says the athletes' crown is "perishable," while ours is "imperishable." The difference is that ours doesn't perish. I'll keep the gold on my base.

Paul doesn't mention kings here. He says they do it "for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable." The difference he names is that ours won't perish. Nothing about who wears it.
Paul says, "I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air." He's picturing a boxer swinging at nothing. Paul wants every swing to land on something.
That's not Paul's picture. He says, "I do not fight like I am beating the air." The man he's describing is swinging, but at nothing. He isn't hiding.
No gate shows up in this verse. Paul says, "I do not fight like I am beating the air." He's talking about swinging with no target. Even my dough gets more of a fight than that.
Paul says, "No, I discipline my body and make it my slave." He starts with the race and the fight, then brings it back to himself. The training he talks about starts with his own body.
Tongue is a good guess, and I've had to bite mine around a cookie jar. But Paul's word is "body." He says, "I discipline my body and make it my slave." The text doesn't name the tongue.

The mind is a fair thing to train, but it isn't Paul's word here. He says, "I discipline my body and make it my slave." The word is body. I think the race picture helps, since runners train their bodies.

explanations.answer: So he won't be disqualified himself
explanations.explanation: Paul says it's "so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified." He's been telling others, and he says he doesn't want to be disqualified himself. It's a humble note to end on, friend.

explanations.answer: So the apostles will take notice
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason. He says it's "so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified." The reason he gives is about not being disqualified himself. The apostles aren't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So the churches will honor him
explanations.explanation: Honor isn't what Paul asks for here. He says, "so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified." That's the reason he gives. Honor from the churches isn't in the verse.
